summary_html: Agency decides to **remove a child immediately** due to **imminent danger** prior to a court order. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) requires later **court findings** on reasonable efforts; constitutional limits (due process; search/seizure) apply.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — monitors safety & removal decision quality

primary_citations.citation_text: New Mexico - NMSA 1978 Chapter 32A, Article 4 (Abuse and Neglect Act: 32A-4-3 duty to report, 32A-4-18 custody hearings, 32A-4-19 adjudicatory hearings), CYFD-published Children's Code compilation (2023 text; 32A-4-3 amended 2025 by SB 42)

New Mexico Statutes Chapter 27 - Public Assistance (public assistance and Medicaid programs; CYFD's child-welfare authority is not in this chapter — it is the Children, Youth and Families Department Act, NMSA 1978 § 9-2A-7(D), and the Children's Code, NMSA 1978 § 32A-1-1, per 8.10.3.3 NMAC)

provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Lowther v. Children Youth and Family Department
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed qualified immunity for the CYFD social worker and county officers who entered a New Mexico home without a warrant and removed two children, and clarified that warrantless entry or seizure in the child welfare context requires a threat of imminent harm under both the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments.
key_cases.relevance: It is the governing circuit authority, decided on New Mexico facts, for whether an emergency removal was constitutionally justified.
key_cases.quote: even in the child welfare context, there must be a threat of imminent harm when officials enter a home or seize children without a warrant or judicial authorization

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court adopted the reasonable-suspicion standard for warrantless emergency removals, holding that officials may remove a child without prior notice and a hearing when they reasonably suspect an immediate threat to the child's safety, that the parents must still receive a prompt post-removal hearing, and that the defendants here did not violate clearly established law and were entitled to qualified immunity.
key_cases.relevance: It supplies the reasonable-suspicion-of-immediate-threat test that governs every warrantless emergency removal in the Tenth Circuit, and it is the framework Lowther later clarifies rather than overrules.
key_cases.quote: officials may remove a child from the home without prior notice and a hearing when they have a reasonable suspicion of an immediate threat to the safety of the child

key_cases.case_name: Malik v. Arapahoe County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed denial of qualified immunity to caseworkers, holding it was clearly established that a parent's liberty interest in familial association cannot be taken without adequate pre-deprivation procedures absent extraordinary circumstances, and that an ex parte order procured by misrepresentation and omission is no substitute.
key_cases.relevance: It is the leading Tenth Circuit decision on the process owed before an emergency removal and on ex parte orders obtained by incomplete affidavits.
key_cases.quote: An ex parte hearing based on misrepresentation and omission does not constitute notice and an opportunity to be heard

key_cases.case_name: State ex rel. Children, Youth & Families Department v. Marlene C. (In re Esther V.)
key_cases.holding: The Court held that in a contested adjudication governed by ICWA the district court must always make the 25 U.S.C. Section 1912(d) and (e) findings at the adjudicatory stage, and separately held that New Mexico's ex parte and custody hearings are Section 1922 emergency proceedings to which Section 1912 does not apply; it reversed the neglect adjudication and remanded.
key_cases.relevance: It squarely addresses the legal status of an emergency removal of an Indian child taken before any Section 1912 findings exist.
key_cases.quote: in a contested adjudication to which ICWA applies, the district court must always make the findings of fact required under § 1912(d) and (e) of ICWA at the adjudication stage

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that a New Mexico CYFD social work supervisor who, together with a deputy sheriff, confronted a student at her high school until she agreed to live with her father violated her clearly established Fourth Amendment right to be free of unreasonable seizure, and reversed the dismissal of her Section 1983 suit.
key_cases.relevance: It holds that a de facto custody change engineered by state officials without judicial authorization is a seizure that must be reasonable.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that she has alleged sufficient facts to demonstrate at the 12(B)(6) stage that she was unreasonably seized within the meaning of the Fourth Amendment

state_agency.name: New Mexico Children, Youth and Families Department

investigation_requirements: A local law enforcement officer trained in the investigation of child abuse and neglect is responsible for investigating reports of alleged child abuse or neglect at schools, daycare facilities or child care facilities (NMSA 1978 § 32A-4-3(C))

If the child alleged to be abused or neglected is in the care or control of CYFD, or in a facility administratively connected to CYFD, the report must be investigated by a local law enforcement officer trained in the investigation of child abuse and neglect (NMSA 1978 § 32A-4-3(D))

timeline_requirements.deadline: 45 days (one supervisor-approved extension of up to 30 additional days)
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Statewide Central Intake accepts the report
